Headline

▌US Senate Fails to Pass Clarity Act Procedural Vote, Ultimately 49 Votes in Favor, 50 Against

On September 16, the US Senate failed to pass the procedural motion for the Clarity Act on September 15, local time, hindering the bill's progress. This vote required 60 votes in favor, and ultimately failed with 49 votes in favor and 50 against.

▌OpenAI Plans Pre-IPO Funding, Targeting a Valuation of $1.2 Trillion

On September 16, according to the Financial Times, OpenAI is in preliminary discussions with investors regarding a new round of private funding, targeting a valuation of approximately $1.2 trillion, in preparation for a future IPO.

According to sources, OpenAI, which completed a funding round in March with a valuation of $852 billion, is discussing further funding plans with major investors due to a recent rebound in market demand driven by its latest AI models. These negotiations are still in the early stages, and the final valuation and funding size may change. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman previously stated that the company's IPO is unlikely before 2027, and believes that the current climate of heightened AI security concerns makes an IPO less than ideal. Reports indicate that OpenAI's revenue growth has accelerated since the release of new models such as GPT-5.6 and Astra, with annualized revenue exceeding $40 billion. The company has previously stated that it has sufficient funds, but training large models still requires significant ongoing capital investment. As of press time, according to CoinGecko data: BTC price is $75,544.02, a 24-hour change of -3.9%; ETH price is $2,397.41, a 24-hour change of -5.8%; BNB price is $711.53, a 24-hour change of -1.4%. The price of SOL is $96.87, a 24-hour change of -5.8%; the price of DOGE is $0.08002, a 24-hour change of -4.9%; the price of XRP is $1.28, a 24-hour change of -10.6%; and the price of ZEC is $1106.40, a 24-hour change of -4.6%. The price of TRX is $0.3328, a 24-hour change of -1.8%; the price of WLFI is $0.05703, a 24-hour change of -1.2%; and the price of HYPE is $76.85, a 24-hour change of -4.6%.

▌Warren Criticizes CLARITY Bill, Claims Trump Family Profited $1.4 Billion from Crypto Last Year

On September 16, U.S. Senator Elizabeth Warren delivered a speech lasting over 10 minutes in the Senate, urging a vote against the CLARITY bill. She stated that Trump and his family profited $1.4 billion from the crypto business by 2025 alone, exceeding the revenue of any publicly traded crypto company in the U.S. last year, while those who purchased their crypto projects lost billions of dollars, including nearly $4 billion in losses for meme buyers. The Senate failed to pass the procedural vote by a vote of 49-50, 11 votes short of the 60 needed to begin debate, with no Democrats voting to advance. Warren claimed the bill would exacerbate Trump's corruption and criticized the ethical clauses negotiated by Republicans with the White House as a "small fig leaf," saying they could not stop Trump from continuing to profit from crypto.

Warren also stated that the bill would tear open huge loopholes in nearly a century of securities law, allowing non-crypto companies to put assets on-chain to circumvent investor protections, and enabling banks to use customer deposits for crypto lending, derivatives trading, node operation, and related software sales. On September 16th, a Fox Business crypto reporter posted on the X platform that US Senator John Kennedy stated he was "not surprised" by the Clarity Act's failure to pass the vote, but did not believe the bill was dead. Kennedy stated that his Democratic colleagues understood the need to develop a cryptocurrency market structure that appeared to be intentionally designed, but that work would have to wait until the lame-duck conference. US Senator Ted Cruz, citing the movie "The Princess Bride," said there was a big difference between a bill that was "dead" and "almost dead," and hoped it would be given a new lease on life. Ted Cruz blamed Democrats for the vote loss, calling them "playing politics" and pushing crypto industry activities and jobs overseas.

▌US House Speaker: AI Bigwigs to Attend Important Meeting at the White House

On September 16, US House Speaker Johnson stated that he spoke with Trump on Monday evening local time, and they are convening executives from artificial intelligence vendors ("all the big names you know") to attend an important meeting at the White House in the coming week. Johnson stated that the way to set up guardrails for AI must be balanced and thoughtful. "I think there needs to be an independent auditing body, and the people developing this technology need to be transparent. There are some very important ideas that can serve as guardrails," he said.

... Blockchain and AI Applications ▌Jensen Huang: AI Security is Crucial, But No New Laws Needed On September 16th, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stated that AI security is crucial, but no new laws are needed. AI companies should control their pace of development until they are confident that their released products will gain market acceptance. ▌Elon Musk Proposes Inter-Company Model Testing Before Release, Advocating Industry Self-Regulation Before Government Regulation On September 15th at the All-In Summit, Elon Musk proposed a new approach to AI security: major AI companies should open their APIs before releasing models, allowing competitors to test each other using their own security testing tools, opposing the practice of "self-grading." He cited recent security incidents, stating that a group of AI agents continuously attacked Hugging Face for a week, even gaining administrator privileges on OpenAI servers, which the latter only noticed a week later; Anthropic has also disclosed security incidents. The "thought processes" of the relevant AI agents show that they actively planned to avoid being detected by humans. Musk stated, "Any sufficiently intelligent model seems to try to break free from its own limitations." Musk expressed agreement with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's assessment of the severity of AI risks, believing that the risks could grow exponentially as the model's capabilities improve. He advocated for industry self-regulation to build a defense before government regulations are implemented, drawing parallels to the MPAA rating system in the US film industry, stating, "There's no need for a UN General Assembly; this can start now." He also believes that if competitors have warned of the model's insecurity and the company still insists on releasing it, it could be direct evidence of negligence. OpenAI: Collaborating with Anthropic and Google on AI Security. OpenAI is collaborating with Anthropic and Google on AI security. Meta Platforms (META.O) will deploy its new self-developed Arke chip in the first half of 2027 and launch its next-generation Astrid chip by the end of 2027, according to market news. Cryptocurrency ▌Bitcoin Electricity Consumption May Have Peaked; December 2025 May Be the Historical Peak On September 15th, Saifedean, author of "Bitcoin Standard," published an article stating that Bitcoin's electricity consumption may have peaked, and it may never consume as much electricity again as it did in 2024-2025. Even if this is not the case, this dynamic is expected to become a reality sometime in the coming years due to mining economics and the halving mechanism. He stated that Bitcoin mining once had a structural long-term tailwind: the value of the block reward increased much faster than the number of Bitcoins reduced by halvings. This tailwind has disappeared. Although the average price of Bitcoin has increased by 2.56 times, the nominal reward income in the current cycle is only 28% higher than the previous cycle; after accounting for the depreciation of the US dollar, the increase is close to zero. Meanwhile, Bitcoin mining difficulty has remained unchanged for 305 days since reaching its all-time high on October 30, 2025, marking the second-longest period without a new high in Bitcoin's history. The Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance estimates that Bitcoin's annualized electricity demand peaks at approximately 190 terawatt-hours (TWh) in December 2025, falling back to the 130 TWh range by mid-2026, while AI is increasing the opportunity cost of high-quality mining infrastructure. Bitcoin's fundamentals suggest it is likely to continue growing, but Bitcoin mining and its electricity consumption may have already peaked. The article also points out that March 14, 2024, could become the day with the highest reward value in Bitcoin mining history, with a price of $73,800 and a block reward of 6.25 BTC, corresponding to a daily reward of approximately $65 million. If the price fails to reach $147,600 before this halving, this will be the first period in which daily mining rewards have not surpassed the previous cycle's high.

▌Ark Invest Reduces Holdings in Crypto Stocks like Circle and Coinbase, Cashing Out Approximately $62 Million in a Single Day

According to The Block, Cathie Wood's Ark Invest reduced its holdings in several crypto stocks on Monday amid a general rise in crypto stocks. Disclosures show that Ark sold 36,628 shares of Coinbase (COIN), worth approximately $7 million based on Monday's closing price of $191.45, with the stock rising 9.24% that day; it also sold a total of 142,350 shares of Circle (CRCL) through two funds, worth approximately $13.8 million, with Circle closing up 7.53% at $97.42.

... In addition, Ark sold 153,881 shares of Bitmine (BMNR, approximately $3.96 million), 18,280 shares of Bullish (BLSH, approximately $688,000), and 1,528,953 shares of its own ARK 21Shares Bitcoin ETF (ARKB), totaling approximately $40 million, the largest single transaction in this round. Ark's adjustment to its crypto holdings is a routine operation, as its investment rules limit a single holding to no more than 10% of the fund portfolio. This market rally coincides with the resumption of Congress and rising market expectations for the Clarity Act to pass this month: Polymarket data shows the probability of the bill's passage rose to 35% yesterday, but fell back to 19% today. The Senate is scheduled to hold a procedural vote at 2:15 PM (Eastern Time) on Tuesday, requiring 60 votes. On September 15th, Lookonchain, an on-chain data agency, reported that Matrixport (@BITofficial_EN) recently deposited 1,400 BTC into Binance, worth approximately $107.8 million; simultaneously, it withdrew 10,000 ETH from Binance, worth approximately $24.67 million. The relevant addresses can be tracked through the Arkham platform. According to common on-chain interpretations, depositing BTC into exchanges is usually seen as a potential signal of selling pressure, while withdrawing ETH from exchanges tends to indicate hoarding. Some market observers believe this operation may involve asset rotation from BTC to ETH, but Matrixport has not yet explained its specific intentions, and the actual use still needs further on-chain verification.

▌A whale closed its short position and then went long on 900 BTC with 40x leverage, holding a position worth nearly $70 million

On September 15th, according to Lookonchain monitoring, a whale closed its short position of 760 BTC, making a profit of $266,000, and then went long on 900 BTC with 40x leverage, worth $69.2 million; this long position currently has a floating profit of $173,000.

▌Multicoin Capital transferred 441,000 HYPE to Coinbase Prime, suspected of selling

According to Jinse Finance, on September 15th, on-chain data agency Onchain Lens monitoring showed that Multicoin Capital transferred 441,000 HYPE to Coinbase Prime through four wallets, worth approximately $35.31 million, most likely in preparation for a sale.

This data can be tracked through the Arkham platform to the corresponding wallet address. As of press time, HYPE and Multicoin have not responded to this.

▌Solana Mainnet Upgrade: Transaction Size Limit Increased from 1232 Bytes to 4096 Bytes

September 15th news, according to Cointelegraph, Solana has increased the maximum transaction size on its mainnet from 1232 bytes to 4096 bytes, more than tripling it. This allows developers to accommodate more complex operations in a single transaction, including zero-knowledge proofs, multi-signature transactions, and new on-chain signature schemes. The upgrade was activated at approximately 1:00 AM UTC on Tuesday at the start of the 1035th epoch of the mainnet, and introduced the v1 transaction format, which is fully backward compatible with the old format. Existing applications and wallets do not need to be modified, but protocols wishing to utilize the larger capacity need to upgrade to the v1 format. A Solana Foundation spokesperson stated that the upgrade aims to unlock workloads that previously could not be accommodated in a single transaction.

... In addition, Solana reduced its block slot time from 400 milliseconds to 350 milliseconds in August, and validators also passed a proposal on August 28 to double the annual deflation rate.

▌Payments startup Velocity raises $48 million in Series A funding, with Visa, Circle, and Ripple participating

On September 15, payments startup Velocity raised $48 million in its Series A funding round, up from $38 million. New investors included Visa, Circle, and Ripple, with Haun Ventures, Translink Capital, and Mirana Ventures also participating, bringing the post-money valuation to $200 million.

▌Singapore's First Locally Tokenized Deposit Payment Completed, DBS, OCBC, and UOB Participate

On September 15, DBS Bank, OCBC Bank, and United Overseas Bank (UOB) completed a locally tokenized deposit payment in Singapore dollars on the SWIFT blockchain ledger. This marks the first time the three institutions have completed an interbank tokenized deposit transaction. The three banks had previously completed cross-border transactions on the SWIFT Ledger. With local interoperability, corporate clients can complete tokenized payments across institutions.

▌Bessenter: We can start paying off debt when the deficit reaches 3% of GDP

US Treasury Secretary Bessenter: We can start paying off debt when the deficit reaches 3% of GDP.

▌The probability of the Fed raising interest rates this week is 92.4%

On September 16, according to CME's "FedWatch": The probability of the Fed keeping interest rates unchanged by September is 7.6%, and the probability of a cumulative rate hike of 25 basis points is 92.4%. The probability of the Fed keeping interest rates unchanged by October is 4%, the probability of a cumulative rate hike of 25 basis points is 52%, and the probability of a cumulative rate hike of 50 basis points is 44%.

Golden Encyclopedia

▌Can Bitcoin Still Be Called "Digital Gold" During Geopolitical Crises?

Every geopolitical crisis causes gold prices to rise while Bitcoin prices plummet. After six tests, the claim of "digital gold" has never been supported by data. Countries hoard gold but exclude Bitcoin from their reserves. For investors, Bitcoin exhibits asymmetry: it falls with stocks but does not rise with them. Three structural asymmetries prevent Bitcoin from achieving safe-haven status: an oversupply of derivatives (market structure), the dominance of leveraged traders (participant composition), and a lack of repeatable behavioral records (behavioral accumulation).

Bitcoin is not a safe-haven asset, but it is a "crisis-useful asset," which can indeed function when borders are closed and banks fail. If these three asymmetries are reduced, Bitcoin may no longer be a replica of gold but rather a completely new "next-generation gold."

Generational shifts and the widespread application of algorithms are key factors that could accelerate this process.

data.title: When Jensen Huang and Dario met Hume: Turkeys, Billiards, and the AI ​​Doomsday Theory
data.description:
01

Recently, the style of the US AI circle is becoming more and more like a reality show.

At the All-In Summit, Professor Huang Renxun spoke eloquently and passionately, stating that the AI ​​doomsday theory is an unscientific sensationalist attempt, and systematically debunked the alarming predictions of the past few years: Radiologists haven't disappeared, in fact, there's a greater shortage; the prediction that 90% of code would be generated by AI didn't happen; the prediction that 50% of entry-level jobs would disappear didn't happen either.

Halfway through his speech, Trump suddenly called!

After a few pleasantries, Teacher Huang emphasized that everything was under his visionary leadership and that they were praising him, before smoothly connecting the microphone to his speaker. The "King of Knowledge's" magnetic voice then resonated throughout the venue, and thousands of audience members heard his pronouncements: the AI ​​doomsday theory is a hoax, a conspiracy by a certain country; data centers are the oil of the future. It's impossible not to suspect this is a classic reality show trope. We often see those unexpected phone calls at crucial moments in dating shows and survival shows. I also think it's very effective at creating atmosphere.

02

However, there are many interesting points here. I carefully examined the argument structure of Huang and Dario and found that no matter which side you support—AI conspiracy theory or AI doomsday theory—their argument structure is consistent:

Huang says that all past doomsday predictions were wrong, therefore current doomsday predictions are also unreliable. ...p>

04

I wonder if everyone has fallen asleep by now. Let's go back to the AI ​​reality show at the beginning:

Huang Renxun said that all past doomsday predictions were wrong, so doomsday theories are unreliable. This argument itself is an inductive method: "Prophets have always been wrong in the past," so "they will be wrong in the future." This is the same as the turkey story. Of course, this doesn't mean he's wrong.

But the doomsday theory is in a more awkward position: "Doomsday" is an event that has never happened.

But the doomsday theory is more awkward: "Doomsday" is an event that has never happened.

Without historical data and constant connections, the probability of "civilization extinction" cannot be proven or disproven; it's closer to a quantifiable expression of subjective belief than a probability in the sense of frequency. Of course, it doesn't mean the probability is zero. Therefore, the inevitable outcome of this argument is political division, because its underlying cause is an epistemological disagreement: when there are no precedents, it's too easy to use it as a political banner. Having done narrative research for a long time, I have a reflexive reaction to situations like this: when neither side can produce decisive evidence, the outcome depends on whose story spreads faster. In conclusion, I think Trump's phone call was definitely not a coincidence. Recently, while pondering the parallel trend hypothesis of difference-in-differences, I've actually developed a sense of respect for it. These seemingly dry theoretical details are actually humanity's efforts to make the "why believe" more solid, even knowing that induction lacks logical guarantees. Perhaps this is a more dignified attitude humanity adopts when facing uncertainty. So, is AI dangerous or not? What's the rush? Thanksgiving isn't even here yet.

data.title: OpenAI President: AGI has already happened.
data.description:
Have you ever considered that AGI (Artificial General Intelligence) has already quietly arrived, but most people haven't realized it yet? Greg Brockman, co-founder and president of OpenAI, recently gave an interview on the a16z podcast, sharing many points that I think are particularly worth considering. One sentence he said really stuck with me: "We've already entered the AGI era." Not the future, not soon, but now, already. He said that Astra (OpenAI's latest flagship model) can already run continuously for 24 hours to complete tasks across a very wide range of fields, which makes him feel that calling it AGI is reasonable. This interview covered several topics, including security, employment, model capabilities, product direction, and entrepreneurial opportunities. After listening, I had many thoughts, and this article is a compilation of those thoughts to discuss with everyone. Ten years ago, they calculated it. In an interview, Greg mentioned that he and Ilya Sutskever had already made a calculation back in 2016 and 2017. They looked at the progress curve of Moore's Law and concluded that if everything went smoothly, AGI would take about 15 years; if they were willing to invest heavily, building supercomputers and spending hundreds of billions of dollars, it might only take 10 years. Now it's 2025, exactly 8 to 9 years since that calculation. Greg said that while everything happening now seems amazing, from a macro perspective, it actually feels like a natural progression; many forces converged at this point in time, making it happen. My own feeling about this viewpoint is that our generation easily underestimates the long-term cumulative effect of technological progress. AGI didn't suddenly fall from the sky one day; it was built bit by bit by countless research teams over the past few decades. Greg and his team were already researching RLHF (Human Feedback Reinforcement Learning) in 2017, thinking about how to supervise a very intelligent system and how to align it with human goals. Those papers didn't get much attention at the time, but they are the foundation of all alignment research today. This makes me realize that truly important work is often done when no one is paying attention, and it may not be seen for ten years. Why are Astra and computer use so important? Greg says that Astra's significant leap forward is largely due to its computer use capability. Computer use means that AI can directly operate the computer interface, using a mouse, keyboard, and screenshots to complete tasks, just like a real person sitting in front of a computer. He explains why this is crucial for AI agents. He says that an agent's usability hinges on two key points: first, whether the model is smart enough to use the tool; and second, whether it can access the necessary contextual information. Before the advent of computer use, everyone was trying to find workarounds—building APIs for AI, building MCP servers (Model Context Protocol servers), and building various CLI (Command Line Interface) interfaces to allow AI to communicate with software. But these methods are essentially patching up the AI, modifying the software into a format that it can barely use. Greg says this approach is cumbersome and awkward, and it introduces additional security risks because each additional interface adds another layer of vulnerability. Computer use takes a completely different approach; it allows AI to directly operate software using a human interface, without needing any special APIs or redesigning any system. He also mentioned that this idea was actually discussed at an internal OpenAI meeting in November 2015. At that time, they were thinking that if the environment for reinforcement learning was screen pixels plus keyboard and mouse input, could anything that could be done on a computer become a training task? He said they had some early attempts at that time, but it wasn't until now that they had truly realized it. I think the significance of computer use is underestimated by most people. It means that AI no longer needs the world to be specially modified for it; instead, it adapts to the existing world. This is a fundamental shift in direction. Previously, humans changed themselves to adapt to software, and then we modified software to adapt to AI, but now AI can finally directly use the interface that humans use. In the long run, this path will go much further because it doesn't rely on any intermediate layer.

10,000 agents solved a mathematical problem

One ​​detail in the interview particularly excited me. Greg mentioned that OpenAI used 10,000 AI agents working in parallel to solve the Navier-Stokes equations problem. This is a problem that has puzzled mathematicians in fluid mechanics for decades, involving how to accurately describe the flow of liquids and gases, and is extremely important for understanding ocean currents, weather systems, aircraft design, and more.

Greg said that they not only solved the problem itself, but also formalized it, writing it in Lean (a mathematical proof language) format.

Greg said that they not only solved the problem itself, but also formalized it, writing it in Lean (a mathematical proof language) format.

In other words, the mathematical proofs written by AI can be verified by machines; they can be proven correct, rather than just "appearing correct." He said the significance of this goes far beyond a single math problem. It represents AI beginning to create new knowledge, not just integrate existing knowledge. New mathematical discoveries will open new doors in science, leading to new drugs, new materials, and new engineering solutions. He said these things are now on the table. My own understanding of this is that every major scientific advancement in human history has been supported by a new set of mathematical tools. Calculus supported classical mechanics, matrices and linear algebra supported quantum mechanics, and probability theory supported statistics and machine learning. If AI begins to autonomously discover new mathematical structures, it may open up scientific directions that we cannot even imagine now. This is not science fiction; the Navier-Stokes example tells us that this has already begun. The window of opportunity for security is closing; time is running out for defenders. Greg spent a significant portion of the interview discussing security issues, particularly the Hugging Face incident. He said this incident made them realize two things. First, AI now possesses very strong cyberattack capabilities; it can discover vulnerabilities, break out of secure environments, and even infiltrate a company's production environment. Second, this capability will eventually spread to more people, including threat actors. His concept of a "defender window" is particularly insightful. This means that currently, such powerful AI security capabilities are only in the hands of a few cutting-edge labs, and ordinary attackers do not yet have these tools. However, this window of opportunity will not last forever. As the technology spreads, attackers will also acquire these capabilities. Therefore, now is the golden period for defenders. You have obtained these tools one step ahead of attackers, and you should use this time to significantly improve your defenses. Greg gave a concrete example, saying that he used Codex (OpenAI's AI programming assistant) to perform a penetration test on his personal website, gregbrockman.com. In 15 minutes, he found 13 security vulnerabilities, including incorrect SPF record settings and the lack of mandatory HTTPS redirects. He then had Codex fix these vulnerabilities. 45 minutes later, Codex automatically opened the cloud console, clicked "operations," set all HTTP security headers, migrated to Cloudflare Pages, started the DMARC (Domain Email Authentication) configuration process, and set up an automated task to return after 48 hours to complete the final step. This example made me realize that a qualitative change is happening in security. Previously, security audits were expensive and slow, requiring specialized teams and significant time investment, making them unaffordable for many small and medium-sized companies. Now, the barrier to entry has been drastically lowered. Greg also mentioned that OpenAI has dedicated 25% of its production engineers to security upgrades, using AI to find vulnerabilities, discovering numerous serious issues, and fixing them all. He said their internal goal is to build a "defense factory," where the entire process—vulnerability discovery → classification → remediation → deployment → verification—is fully automated, operating at machine speed. Once achieved, defenders will be far more efficient than attackers, because attackers need to find vulnerabilities one by one, while defenders can go through the entire codebase. OpenAI also announced a $1 billion Frontline Defenders program to provide free or discounted AI security tools to organizations that lack the purchasing power, such as hospitals, water companies, and government critical infrastructure. I think this is the right direction, because security vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure are vulnerabilities in the entire society, and cannot be solved solely by commercial logic. The true form of AI has not yet emerged. There was a quote from Greg in the interview that resonated with me the most. He said that ChatGPT and ChatGPT Work are essentially text boxes. The new text boxes are much stronger than the old ones, but they are still text boxes. This is not the kind of AI we have been promised. He said that true AI should be like this: you primarily communicate with it through voice, but typing is also possible; it has persistent memory and knows who you are; it is proactive, not just waiting for you to ask questions, but actively helping you discover and solve problems; it can help you in both your personal and professional life; and you can truly rely on it. He also mentioned that OpenAI now has over 1 billion weekly active users, but there are still approximately 1.5 billion users who have used ChatGPT and then abandoned it. He said this group is very important; they tried it but weren't retained, possibly because the AI ​​wasn't good enough at the time, or perhaps they didn't know how to use it. Here he raises a very interesting point: AI shouldn't leave users to figure out what it can do, but rather proactively tell users, "I can help you with this." Currently, many people's use of AI is still at the stage of "I try to ask it something," rather than "It's a true collaborator in my daily workflow." I personally resonate deeply with this view. I've met many people who are fully capable of using AI, but they use it very superficially. The reason isn't that AI is bad, but that they don't know where to start, or in which scenarios this tool can bring them real value. This problem cannot be solved by users figuring it out on their own; it must be proactively guided at the product level. Greg says their North Star is "simplicity," truly integrating AI into your life, rather than making you revolve around AI. I think this is a very sober assessment, and it's also where most AI products still have a long way to go. Regarding the employment issue, nobody really knows the answer. Greg said something I really admired in an interview when discussing employment: he said that the history of AI development tells us that it almost never develops according to logical deduction, even when the conclusion seems very inevitable. His basic stance is that humans will not lose their ability to create value because of AI. He said accountability is a very fundamental example—setting goals and taking responsibility for results—these are things that humans should retain, not because AI can't do them, but because human value is not just about completing tasks, but about existing as human beings. He said he believes we will enter a wave of entrepreneurship because AI has significantly lowered the barriers to entry into an industry and starting a business. He heard that a group of people are quitting their jobs to start their own businesses because they feel they can do more with AI tools. My own thoughts on employment are: every major technological revolution in history has brought anxiety about "this job will disappear," but in reality, after each technological revolution, humanity has found new ways of working, and overall living standards have improved. Agricultural mechanization reduced the demand for agricultural labor, but it gave people time to do other things; industrialization created a large number of new jobs. The real question is not whether jobs will disappear, but whether the pace of transformation is slow enough to allow people time to adapt. This is what I think is truly worrying, not the relatively unfounded question of whether AI will replace all human jobs. How He Decides Where to Spend His Time In the final part of the interview, Greg discussed how he allocates his energy. He said that throughout his years at OpenAI, he has always followed one principle: focus on the most important problem, the one that might not have happened without him. For the past two years, that problem has been data centers, infrastructure, and machine learning engineering. He said they invested heavily in pre-training infrastructure to get the research moving at a real pace. This year, the problem has become business: how to truly bring the technology to the world and make it a product reality. They canceled the Sora project this year, a painful decision he said, but necessary to free up the company's focus. He used an analogy from the book *The Score Takes Care of Itself*: You don't win the Super Bowl by shouting "I'm going to win!"; you win by every block, every tackle. You can only influence the input, not the result, so focus on the basics. He also described a detail of his management style: he likes to "lead from the trenches," deeply understanding specific situations and constantly asking, "Does this make sense? I don't quite understand this part." He said he encountered some difficult-to-explain issues in the past few days, and his approach was to gather everyone who had a different perspective on the issue on a phone call, look at a Google Doc together, and discuss line by line: Is this sentence correct? What are we really trying to say? I think there's a very important understanding behind this approach: when something is unclear, it's usually not because it's too complex, but because it hasn't been truly thought through. Forcing it into a comprehensible text is itself a form of forced thinking. This is a habit I'm gradually developing myself. My final thoughts: After listening to the entire interview, I think Greg is a very clear-headed person overall. He doesn't exaggerate, doesn't shy away from difficulties, and is unsure about things he's uncertain about, but very firm about things he's certain about. One sentence he said has stuck with me: the progress of AI almost never follows logical deduction. The other side of this statement is: your predictions about the future of AI, whether pessimistic or optimistic, are most likely wrong, and in ways you didn't expect. What truly matters isn't making correct predictions, but maintaining sufficient openness to quickly absorb new information and adjust your judgment. We now live in an era where everyone can use AI, but only a minority truly utilize it effectively and create value. This gap isn't about the tools, but about cognition and practice. The AGI era has arrived, but most people don't yet understand what this means, and this is perhaps the most worthwhile thing to figure out right now.
